summary.text: Mineral properties are the traits used to describe a mineral species, from its chemistry and crystal structure to features like hardness, lustre, colour, streak and cleavage.
A mineral's ordered arrangement of atoms gives rise to visible properties such as its crystal form, hardness and cleavage.
Structure counts as much as chemistry: quartz and stishovite are both silicon dioxide, yet their different crystal structures make them two minerals.

facts.label: Common properties
facts.value: Habit, hardness, lustre, streak, cleavage, magnetism, fluorescence

facts.label: Unusual tests
facts.value: Taste, smell and reaction to acid

facts.label: Ice versus water
facts.value: Water ice is a mineral; liquid water is not

items.prompt: Two natural samples are both pure silicon dioxide, but their atoms are arranged in different crystal structures. How do mineralogists count them?

options.label: As one mineral in two forms
As one mineral and one rock
As two different mineral species
As not minerals at all

items.explain: Each crystal structure of a compound is its own species, which is why quartz and stishovite are separate minerals.

items.prompt: Obsidian is a natural volcanic glass whose atoms have no orderly crystal pattern. How is it classified?

options.label: As a mineraloid
As a mineral, since it is natural
As a biogenic mineral
As a type of quartz

items.explain: Minerals need an ordered atomic arrangement, so amorphous natural solids like obsidian are called mineraloids.

items.prompt: A frozen pond has a sheet of ice on top and liquid water beneath. Which of these counts as a mineral?

options.label: Both, because they are the same substance
Only the liquid water
Neither, because water is a compound
Only the ice

items.explain: A mineral must be solid in its natural occurrence, so water is not a mineral but water ice is.

items.prompt: Mercury is a liquid at room temperature, yet it is still listed as an official mineral. Why?

options.label: It is solid deep inside the Earth
It was listed before the current rules existed
Liquid metals are exempt from the solid rule
It always occurs inside other crystals

items.explain: Native mercury crystallizes only below −39 °C, but it keeps its status because it was included before the current rules.

items.prompt: A newly found natural substance has a definite crystal structure but is stable only below 2 °C. Can it be recognized as a mineral?

options.label: No, minerals must be stable at room temperature
No, it must first be found on another planet
Only if it can be made in a laboratory
Yes, if its structure and makeup can be determined

items.explain: The IMA only asks that a substance be stable enough to pin down its structure and composition; meridianiite is accepted though stable only below 2 °C.

items.prompt: Why does each mineral have its own typical hardness and way of breaking, rather than varying at random?

options.label: Its atoms sit in an ordered arrangement
It always forms at the same temperature
Living things shape it as it grows
It is always found inside the same rock

items.explain: A mineral's ordered atomic arrangement implies properties such as crystal form, hardness and cleavage.
